actions.justification: MANDATORY: Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both major risk factors for contrast-induced AKI. Hydration status must be assessed prior to cardiac catheterization to guide pre-procedural IV fluid administration.

MANDATORY: Baseline eGFR is essential for risk stratification of contrast-induced nephropathy. CKD stage 4 implies significantly reduced GFR (15-29 mL/min/1.73m²), which markedly increases CI-AKI risk and guides decisions on contrast volume and pre-hydration.

MANDATORY: Systematic review of risk factors (CKD stage 4, diabetes, concurrent nephrotoxins, hemodynamic status) is required to calculate CI-AKI risk score and plan appropriate preventive strategies before contrast administration.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is scheduled for cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure. Assessing current vital signs establishes a baseline before the procedure and identifies any hemodynamic instability that could increase CI-AKI risk.

Review current medications to identify nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, metformin) that should be held before contrast administration in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume limit based on eGFR (already obtained) to minimize contrast-induced AKI risk in this CKD stage 4 patient undergoing cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Before proceeding with contrast-based cardiac catheterization, alternative imaging modalities (e.g., CO2 angiography, MRI) should be considered to minimize nephrotoxin exposure.

CKD stage 4 with diabetes significantly increases risk of contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is indicated to guide pre-procedural optimization, hydration strategy, and post-procedure monitoring.

Patient is at high risk for contrast nephropathy given CKD stage 4 and diabetes. All nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors, etc.) should be held or avoided peri-procedurally to reduce cumulative renal injury risk.
Formally document the baseline eGFR for this CKD stage 4 patient prior to contrast exposure; essential for post-procedure comparison to detect CIN.
Urine output assessment is critical in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient to ensure adequate hydration before contrast administration and establish a pre-procedure baseline.
Discontinuing nephrotoxic medications (e.g., NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) before cardiac catheterization reduces additive nephrotoxic risk in this high-risk CKD+diabetes patient.

Patient has diabetes and is on metformin. Per guidelines, metformin should be held before contrast administration in patients with CKD (eGFR <45-60) due to risk of lactic acidosis if AKI develops post-contrast.

IV isotonic crystalloid hydration (0.9% NaCl or sodium bicarbonate) is the cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Should be initiated pre-procedure and continued peri- and post-procedure.
Post-contrast SCr at 48 hours is recommended to detect contrast-induced AKI early, especially in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes. Scheduling this now ensures follow-up is not missed.
Patient has CKD stage 4 — all nephrotoxic medications must be held prior to contrast administration to minimize risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.

Patient has CKD stage 4 (GFR likely <45, i.e., G3b or worse) and diabetes. Metformin should be held at the time of contrast administration and for 48 hours post-procedure due to risk of lactic acidosis.
IV hydration (isotonic saline or sodium bicarbonate) is the most evidence-based intervention for CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients with CKD and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, placing them at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedural IV hydration (isotonic saline) is a key evidence-based intervention to reduce CI-AKI risk before cardiac catheterization.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD/diabetic patient undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of acute kidney injury and guide hydration adequacy.
Serial serum creatinine monitoring at 48-72 hours post-contrast is guideline-recommended to detect contrast-induced nephropathy, given the patient's CKD stage 4 and diabetic risk factors.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Checking serum creatinine at 72 hours post-contrast is essential to detect delayed AKI, as pre/post hydration has been given and baseline eGFR was documented.

CKD stage 4 with diabetes represents very high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology input is warranted to guide ongoing renal protection strategy, assess need for RRT preparation, and optimize fluid management post-procedure.

Ongoing optimization of fluid status in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient is critical to maintain adequate renal perfusion post-contrast exposure and mitigate risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
